results.question: Compare what the book says about making your own chroma keyer with what it says about nons
results.answer:
The book treats these two subjects as opposite kinds of problems: a chroma keyer is something you're told not to bother building yourself, while nonsquare pixels are a format condition you can't avoid and must handle deliberately. The shared lesson underneath both is that the representation a system works in differs from what the eye sees — keying happens in HSV space rather than RGB, and rectangular pixel data is unsqueezed only for display, never modified [S4][S6].

| Aspect | Making your own chroma keyer | Nonsquare pixels |
|---|---|---|
| Core concept | A tool that turns a chosen hue/saturation/luminance range into a matte [S3][S6] | Pixels whose width differs from height, measured as pixel aspect ratio [S9] |
| Book's stance | DIY discouraged — off-the-shelf keyers are hard to improve upon [S1] | Not optional; you must handle the format correctly [S7] |
| Key representation lesson | Keying is done in HSV, since saturation isn't an RGB attribute [S6] | Display is unsqueezed but the underlying data is unchanged [S4] |
| Main pitfall | Terrible edge blending on greenscreen hair; keyers are only for garbage mattes there [S14] | Rotating a squeezed image without unsqueezing first distorts it [S15] |

**Making your own chroma keyer**

A chroma keyer defines pixels within a selected range of color and brightness as background: a starting pixel value marks the center of the key, pixels inside the Hue/Saturation/Value ranges become white, pixels outside become black, and tolerance settings produce a soft edge [S6][S3]. The recipe for building one is simple in principle: convert RGB to HSV, pipe it through a color curve, and remember that the red curve now carries Hue, green carries Saturation, and blue carries Value (brightness) [S2].

The book's verdict, though, is that this is more hassle than it's worth — unlike the luma key, where cleverness can genuinely beat the basic design, an off-the-shelf chroma keyer is hard to improve upon [S1]. It also flatly warns against using a chroma keyer for greenscreen work except to pull garbage mattes, because it fails on edge-blended pixels like wisps of hair [S14]. A more exotic DIY alternative is a three-dimensional color keyer that works in RGB cube space on any arbitrary color, using a grossly simplified version of Primatte's operating principles [S8].

**Nonsquare pixels**

A nonsquare pixel is one whose width and height are unequal; the ratio is expressed as a pixel aspect ratio [S9][S5]. Standard-definition video uses these rectangular pixels — 720×480 for NTSC-DV and 720×576 for PAL-DV — while HD, graphics software, and computer monitors all use square pixels [S10]. Systems that display such images apply a temporary geometric "unsqueeze" so the image looks as it will in final form; the stored image data itself is not altered [S4].

The practical implications surface in compositing operations, most dramatically with anamorphic formats like Cinemascope's 2:1 squeeze [S7]. If you rotate an element while it's still squeezed, the result is distorted once it's unsqueezed — the correct order is unsqueeze, rotate, then resqueeze along the x-axis [S15]. Even a small 5° rotation shows a subtle error on a round subject, so the book's advice is to double-check everything when working with nonsquare pixels [S15].

One aspect of the request — how a digital image represents spatial dimensions more generally — has no relevant coverage in the retrieved evidence, so no comparison is possible there.

results.question: Compare what the book says about miscellaneous drawing tips with what it says about transc
results.answer:
The two topics come from different books and sit at opposite ends of the color-reproduction spectrum: the manga drawing guide offers hands-on, subjective tips for making an illustration look better, while the VES Handbook describes mathematically rigorous procedures for making an image look *correct* on a different display.

**The drawing tips** (from *Complete Guide to Drawing Dynamic Manga Sword Fighters*, [S4]) are about aesthetic experimentation before finishing a piece. If the color isn't to your liking, swap in alternate colors to find a stronger combination, and add effects — for example, bright circles around the character — by creating a new luminescence layer. The advice is intuitive, trial-and-error, and aimed at a single artwork's visual appeal.

**Transcoding versus color rerendering** (from the *VES Handbook of Visual Effects*, [S1][S2]) addresses converting image data between displays. The choice depends on how dissimilar the displays are:

- **Transcoding** fits when displays match in black levels, white luminance, viewing conditions, and gamma, but differ in primary chromaticities: linearize the first display's encoded RGB, convert to CIE XYZ, convert to the second display's RGB, then reimpose the encoding nonlinearity [S2].
- **Color rerendering** fits when contrast, white levels, or viewing conditions are grossly dissimilar: undo whatever color rendering was done for the first display, then color render the neutral CIE XYZ values for the second display [S1].

The unifying idea is that *any* conversion "has the goal of making the colors… match as closely as possible" [S3], and color rendering itself means transforming an image to account for differences in viewing environment — e.g., JPEG output-referred images from a camera are color rendered to compensate for the gap between desert sunlight and an office monitor [S5].

| Aspect | Drawing tips (manga guide) | Transcoding vs. rerendering (VES Handbook) |
|---|---|---|
| Goal | Make one artwork more pleasing | Reproduce colors faithfully across displays |
| Method | Subjective color swaps, extra effect layers | Linearization, CIE XYZ conversion, re-encoding |
| Mindset | Artistic experimentation | Precision math grounded in display physics |
| Output | A "stronger" illustration | Correct image data for a target display |

Both are creative in their own way — the transcoding path is constrained by display physics (gamma, primaries, viewing conditions), while the drawing tips are constrained only by taste.

One gap: the evidence contains nothing on how a system preserves or alters original data through interpretation during these conversions — that aspect isn't covered in the retrieved material.

results.question: Compare what the book says about transcoding versus color rerendering with what it says ab
results.answer:
The VES Handbook draws a clear line between transcoding and color rerendering, but that comparison has no counterpart to weigh it against: nothing in the retrieved corpus mentions FACE OFF at all, so that half of the question is missing evidence rather than a divergent book position.

When two displays differ only in their primary chromaticities, the book describes **transcoding** as a mechanical conversion: linearize the first display's encoded RGB values, convert them to CIE XYZ, convert those XYZ values to the second display's RGB values, and reimpose the encoding nonlinearity [S2]. This works only because black level, white luminance, gamma, and viewing conditions are assumed identical — no interpretation enters, XYZ is just a bridge between two known device encodings.

**Color rerendering** covers the harder case. Color rendering itself is defined as transforming an image to account for differences in viewing environment — a still camera, for instance, renders a desert-sunlit scene into an sRGB or Adobe RGB JPEG aimed at a dim office monitor [S3]. When contrast, white levels, or viewing conditions differ grossly, the book says the best solution is to undo the first display's color rendering, recover the non-color-rendered CIE XYZ scene values, and color render them afresh for the second display [S1]. Doing the rendering is easier than undoing it, which is why raw encodings leave it to the downstream team while baked-in camera rendering is hard to reverse [S4].

| Aspect | Transcoding | Color rerendering |
|---|---|---|
| Trigger | Displays differ only in primaries [S2] | Contrast, white level, or viewing conditions differ grossly [S1] |
| Operation | Linearize → XYZ → new RGB → re-encode [S2] | Undo old rendering → XYZ scene values → render for new display [S1] |
| Interpretation | None — a pure numeric mapping | Perceptual adaptation to a viewing environment [S3] |

Notice that both routes pass through CIE XYZ; the difference is whether the first display's rendering is carried across or deliberately undone. The same split shows up in the workflow material: ACES keeps the colorist's "look" in the RRT and re-renders it for each device via ODTs, with gamut mapping flagged as the remaining problem for low-gamut HDTV [S11], and scene-referred OpenEXR frames must be transformed at load time or in a GPU shader before playback [S5].

As for FACE OFF, the corpus contains no discussion of it — no reference to the film and no face-replacement treatment under that name. The facial content that does appear is unrelated: FACS scoring instructions [S12][S13], a 2025 facial-expression-editing paper [S6], and compositing tips on morphing a face to non-face targets such as a car or baseball [S8]. The missing premise is the source itself: if you can name the book and chapter that discusses FACE OFF, I can pull that passage and run the comparison directly.

results.question: Compare what the book says about affect, fatigue, and injury are control states with what
results.answer:
The two threads treat movement from opposite ends of the causal chain. Your handbook's §6.1 and combat-state tables treat **affect, fatigue, and injury as control states** — internal conditions that must change later action selection and execution, "not adjectives appended after choreography is chosen" [S8]. The visual-structure sources in the corpus (Bruce Block, the VES Handbook, Mascelli) instead treat an object's movement against a background as something the eye reconstructs from relative motion — including motion that is not actually happening [S5].

## The control-state view

Each state has a structured schema with fields, units, and update triggers [S7]:

- **Affect** updates through appraisal: a trigger (e.g., "expected interception fails and north lane opens") is scored on goal congruence, controllability, and certainty, and then alters valence, arousal, and dominance, with behavioral effects such as narrowed attention, urgent-but-less-clean recovery, and higher risk tolerance for one attempt [S8]. Movement-facing affect fields include initiation latency, preferred interpersonal distance, acceleration profile, posture amplitude, gaze allocation, willingness to accept unstable support, and recovery patience versus urgency [S3].
- **Fatigue** is factored into global exertion and local capacity — RPE 0–10, breath cycle, recovery rate, plus per-limb capacity — with coordination effects like increased step-width variability, longer stabilization after hard redirection, and greater trunk contribution when a shoulder is taxed [S12][S7].
- **Injury** must specify mechanical consequences and compensations: pain 0–10, severity 0–4, reduced load acceptance, flexion tolerance, and push-off capacity, compensated by favoring the right leg, shortening the left stance interval, and increasing trunk lean during emergency recovery — all with an explicit uncertainty and confidence level [S1][S7].

## The object-with-background view

Here the sources describe how movement is perceived, not what causes it:

- **Induced movement:** a moving object transfers its movement to a nearby stationary object, so the stationary object appears to move and the moving object appears stationary [S5].
- **Quality affinity:** when an object moves in the same direction and curve across shots, the visual intensity reads as low [S2].
- **Match moving:** when the foreground camera moves, the background must move appropriately; tracking data extracted from the foreground image is applied to the background during compositing [S11].
- **Motion parallax:** players and camera moving past foreground objects create a variation in image travel at different distances that conveys position and distance to the viewer [S13].

## The comparison

| Dimension | Affect / fatigue / injury | Object movement vs. background |
|---|---|---|
| Nature | Internal, functional state | Perceptual appearance |
| Temporal direction | Forward — shapes future action selection | Outward — shapes what the viewer reads from the image |
| Representation | State schemas (fields, units, update triggers) | Camera and compositing technique |
| Function | Decides what movement should occur | Decides what movement appears to occur |
| Status | Causal mechanism | Can be illusory (induced movement) |

The two views connect where a control state becomes visible: injury compensations (favoring right-leg support, shortened stance, trunk lean) and affect effects (urgent recovery, narrowed attention) alter precisely the kinematics that the perceptual sources explain how to stage and read [S1][S8]. The corpus's Laban-based material sits between the two — it treats kinematic and expressive characteristics themselves as the carrier of affect, as in the HMM-over-Laban generation approach [S4]. One step the sources do not articulate is the general mechanism linking an internal state to its observable behavior; the link appears only through these worked examples.

results.question: Compare what the book says about movement of an object with a background with what it says
results.answer:
Both the movement texts and the sound-editing texts in this corpus run on the same perceptual logic — layered figure and background, continuity across the cut, and proximity that must be rendered consistently — but each domain expresses that logic in its own vocabulary. The movement material comes mainly from Bruce Block's *The Visual Story* and the VES Handbook, while the sound principles come from *Grammar of the Edit*, Murch, Lumet, and Rabiger, so the comparison is across the corpus rather than within a single book.

| Dimension | Object movement vs. background | Sound editing | Shared principle |
|---|---|---|---|
| Layering | Adding FG/BG objects increases alternation, repetition, and tempo; a moving object passing a stationary object strengthens that existing visual beat [S2] | Sound editors think in both dimensions at once: a horizontal stream of sounds plus vertical layers — freeway, birds, plane, footsteps — woven into a "multidimensional tapestry" [S3]; sounds can jump between figure and background levels [S12] | Figure–ground composition is the basic organizing structure of both channels |
| Continuity across the cut | Shot-to-shot motion must continue: the movement in Shot #2 begins where Shot #1's movement ended [S7] | Diegetic sound carries over the cut (the airplane stays audible, slightly lowered, even when off-screen); walla tracks run continuously under multiple cuts to blend them [S4][S6] | A cut is masked by preserving the perceptual signature that started before it |
| Proximity / perspective | A close-up magnifies the visual size and importance of an object [S10] | Levels and panning are mixed to match distance from the action and narrative importance; the CU teakettle whistle gets louder to match its magnified image [S1][S10] | Shot size is mapped onto loudness — the audio stands in for visual distance |
| Background response to foreground | In compositing, when the foreground camera moves the background must move appropriately, via match moving; in virtual studios this alignment is automated after calibration [S9][S11] | Quieter dialogue backgrounds are augmented to match noisier ones, and room tone fills gaps left by dialogue cutting [S8] | Background must adapt to foreground or the illusion breaks — geometrically in visuals, in level terms in audio |
| Handling change | Passing a stationary object makes an existing beat stronger, a gradual intensification [S2] | Because "the ear registers a sound cut more readily than a graduated change," ambience changes are done as sound dissolves rather than hard cuts [S8] | Graduated transitions read as purposeful; abrupt ones read as errors |

```
Movement:  FG object ──passes──► stationary BG  →  beat strengthened (S2)
           motion continues across cut, same trajectory (S7)
Sound:     figure layer ──passes──► ambience layer  →  level/focus shift (S12)
           ambience carries across cut, slightly lowered (S4, S6)
```

Where they genuinely differ is in emphasis. The movement writing frames everything as rhythm and tempo — beats, repetition, alternation — a time-based musicality, while the sound writing is dominated by spatial concerns: perspective, proximity, panning, and matching ambience from angle to angle [S1][S8][S10]. Sound also has a privilege movement lacks: it can hold the scene together across cuts even when the image no longer shows the source, so an off-screen airplane or a continuing walla bed literally stitches shots together [S4][S6]; the visual counterpart is only the *continuum* rule that motion should pick up where it left off [S7].

One caveat: the retrieved sources do not cover how a change in one sensory channel directly affects perception of the other — the parallels above are structural, inferred from how each domain is independently described, not demonstrated cross-modal effects. There is also no treatment in the evidence of surround-sound technique, which *Grammar of the Edit* explicitly defers as beyond its scope [S1].

results.question: Compare what the book says about sound editing with what it says about write radio sparely
results.answer:
Both books land on the same principle from opposite ends of the process: **sound editing** is a post-production craft that carves meaning out of recorded material, while **spare radio writing** is a pre-production discipline of omission. Yet each advises the same thing — the less you use, the more the work communicates.

| Aspect | Sound editing says | Spare radio writing says |
|---|---|---|
| Core rule | Start from the cleanest, clearest, strongest signal; degrade it only deliberately for effect [S6] | Write sparely — bare-bones execution leaps out of the radio [S2][S3] |
| Silence / absence | No more dialogue than absolutely necessary, so effects and music have room [S11] | Silence is radio's white space; it enlarges the idea it surrounds [S2] |
| Sound effects | Enhance SFX tracks to establish the appropriate atmosphere [S11] | SFX can be the story, but don't overuse them or expect them to do what they can't [S7] |
| Goal | Believability of performance and story progression [S8] | One simple, clean, easily comprehended core message [S13] |
| Constraint | Must parallel the picture edit and serve the narrative [S8] | No visual graphic standards; spots can stand alone [S14] |

**Where they agree.** Both disciplines treat restraint as the engine of meaning. The sound editor's final pass asks whether every line of dialogue is necessary, and what's cut creates space for atmosphere and music to carry the scene [S11]; the radio writer builds that same sparseness in from the first draft, letting the voice talent read slowly and quietly, one word at a time [S3]. Both also distrust effects as a crutch — sound effects in radio "can be the story," but overuse breaks them [S7], and in film editing effects are enhanced only to establish atmosphere, never to replace narrative [S11].

**Where they differ.** Sound editing reshapes what already exists — gathering wild tracks like a clean, close recording of a car door slam, then selecting and refining them in phases: the rough cut pursues realism and believability, while dramatic emphasis, metaphor, and music belong to the fine cut [S10][S8][S11]. Radio writing creates from nothing, so the sparseness must be composed, not carved out later. The sound editor is also bound to the picture, seeking narrative exposition parallel to the visual edit [S8], while the radio writer faces no visual standards at all and can attack the brief one spot at a time [S14]. The sharpest contrast is in how each treats the material: editing permits controlled degradation — starting clean and worsening the sound on purpose for an effect [S6] — whereas spare radio writing is pure omission. There's nothing to degrade.

results.question: Compare what the book says about write radio sparely with what it says about rewards of go
results.answer:
The two ideas come from different books — **Hey Whipple Squeeze This** is talking about a craft rule for writing ads, while **Gifts Differing** is talking about a lifelong developmental outcome — yet both land on the same underlying economy: maximum effect from minimum excess.

**Writing radio sparely** means using as few words as the concept allows, so the voice talent can read slowly, quietly, one word at a time [S2]. The practical method is to write and time the mandatory copy first, then fit the commercial into whatever time is left; overwriting is called "the most common mistake," and the cure is to underwrite [S5]. The theory behind it is that silence functions in radio the way white space does in print — it enlarges the idea it surrounds [S10].

**The rewards of good type development**, by contrast, are the payoff of a whole life structure: well-developed perception and judgment have "a wide range and profound influence on effectiveness, success, happiness, and mental health" [S1]. The boldest claim is that type development can substitute for intelligence — average intelligence, fully utilized through fine type development, produces results far above expectation, while a serious deficit of judgment is a disability no amount of intelligence can compensate [S7]. Development is fueled by rewards matched to each type: possessions for a sensing child, freedoms for an intuitive, dignity or authority for a thinker, praise or companionship for a feeling type [S6].

| Dimension | Writing radio sparely | Rewards of type development |
|---|---|---|
| Nature | A craft rule for copywriting | A developmental outcome of personality |
| Core move | Subtraction — cut words to create silence [S10] | Cultivation — build perception and judgment over time [S7] |
| Enemy | Overwriting [S5] | Deficit of development, especially of judgment [S7] |
| Reward | The idea is enlarged; the listener fills the space [S9][S10] | Effectiveness, success, happiness, mental health [S1] |
| Timescale | Immediate — a 30- or 60-second spot [S3] | Lifelong, from babyhood through adulthood [S15] |

Where they agree: both treat restraint as the engine of power, not the absence of it — spare radio lets silence enlarge the idea, and developed judgment focuses even average intelligence on "the necessary things at the necessary times" [S7][S10]. Both also assume the effect depends on fit with the receiver: radio draws on the listener's imagination to make a message personal [S9], just as type development requires the right incentive for the right disposition [S6].

Where they part ways: radio spareness is a prescriptive production discipline — do the mandatories first, time them, underwrite — while type development is a descriptive variable with a wide range that can "substitute for intelligence" or, if neglected, constitute a disability [S5][S7]. Spare writing aims at a single message landing in 30 or 60 seconds and depends on frequency to work [S14], whereas type development is about a trajectory that compounds over a lifetime [S15]. One is a technique for a moment of attention; the other is a theory of a whole person.

One gap in the evidence: the corpus never explains **how a writer chooses what to include or omit** to serve the story — radio spareness is given only as a rule, not a decision procedure, so that aspect of the comparison has no basis in the retrieved material.
